However, in that case it has to be very careful not to trigger these EU rules because products move through Northern Ireland.
If I were a Tunbridge Wells widget manufacturer—although I am not sure that there are many of those—and I sold some widgets to Northern Ireland, I would fall within EU state aid rules.

Yes. It is a matter of scale and it is also a question of whether that manufacturer would qualify for an exemption from EU state aid rules in general, as some things are exempted. Again, this is likely to end up in arbitration in one way or another, the question being: how does it affect trade between Northern Ireland and the EU?

The flipside of that is that if the UK Government decided to give, outside the EU, a form of state aid that would not be permissible inside the EU but was outside the EU, Northern Irish firms could not get that form of state aid.
Not without falling foul of the rules.
So they will be excluded from a UK form of subsidy that is prohibited by EU state aid rules.
Unless they can demonstrate in one way or another that the subsidy they are getting has no impact on trade between Ireland and Northern Ireland.
In answer to Lord Wood, you talked about the widgets just being sold to Northern Ireland. You do not mean that they have to go from Northern Ireland into the EU?

No, not necessarily, because there will be a competitive disadvantage. If the widget is sponsored by the UK and can be sold for only £10 in Northern Ireland, whereas the equivalent subsidy does not exist in the EU, so a similar widget produced in Amsterdam or Dublin will be much more expensive, we are in state aid territory. It is about ensuring level competition between Northern Ireland and Ireland because the product is moving within that single market territory.

Interestingly, because of where this fits within the P rotocol on Ireland and Northern Ireland, companies dealing with these rules could, in an England and Wales court case, still potentially make a preliminary reference to the Court of Justice of the European Union over state aid elements because of their effects on the P rotocol on Ireland/Northern Ireland.

I am struck by how wide the definition of state aid in Annexe 5 to the P rotocol is. It includes all sorts of stuff: training aid, employment aid, regional aid, and so on. In GB, aid to a company in Aberdeen could be banned if the goods it produced were at risk of going into the EU, or one could end up in court on infringement proceedings because of that aid. I find it hard to see how it will work out in practice but, in theory, this state aid article is very wide-ranging.
Yes, it is. I w ould suggest that, to play it safe, the UK Government might in general wish to keep EU state aid rules in mind when deciding on any subsidies.
I am sorry that we are running out of time, but I would like to bring in Baroness Brown on this point.

Q14 Given that very broad definition of state aid, could there be a danger in the UK Government trying to replace some of the support that has come through the European Regional Development Fund, which might support a company in Wales or somewhere with R&D or training? Now that we are no longer in the EU, could something that replaced that be regarded as state aid?

Yes. Off the top of my head, the only exception noted in the P rotocol is agricultural subsidies to farmers in Northern Ireland. Those would be exempted from the EU state aid rules, as far as I am aware, under certain conditions which I think are to be defined by the J oint C ommittee. The J oint C ommittee is not busy enough yet, so it is also working on that.
So is there potential that our CAP replacement in Great Britain could be regarded as state aid, depending on what precisely it does?

The point of Article 10(2) is to avoid that being an issue and ensure that whatever replaces the CAP is not prohibited because of the P rotocol on Northern Ireland. I think that is the only type of subsidy that was negotiated on.
But regional development funding is innately different—
We are very short of time, so I would like to turn to another very important subject.

Q15 This is telling. You started to touch on the issue of the potential, putative EU-UK free trade agreement and its impact on the P rotocol. I think you said that there would be a sigh of relief if all tariffs were abolished as part of that agreement; that would certainly simplify things. Would a free trade agreement have any other impacts on the operation of the P rotocol, beyond that yes or no on tariffs? If we do not get a free trade agreement, are there any other aspects apart from tariffs that would have an impact?

Essentially, all the checks between the European Union, Northern Ireland and Great Britain can be reduced or eliminated through a free trade agreement. So, for example, regulatory alignment is an obvious one. I know that the Government are saying that there will not be any alignment, but if there is, that could potentially reduce the level of checks.

Typically, within EU trade agreements, and certainly within the EU-Canada agreement, you have some kind of equivalence regime with checks on food-related products, which reduces the checks on those considerably. It actually lays out the percentage of products which will be checked, which can be as low as 1% or 2%. That would be of great assistance as well.

Procedures to simplify customs can also be agreed in trade agreements. For example, one can mutually recognise authorised economic operators, which would also help reduce the checks. Many things can be included which would help trade between not only Great Britain and Northern Ireland but Dover and Calais, for example. I take Dover and Calais as my starting point, as we will have to invent something like that for trade between Northern Ireland and Great Britain. So if we simplify that, we would also simplify the checks between Northern Ireland and Great Britain.

Putting it the other way around, if the Government do what they say they will do and move towards regulatory divergence in whatever free trade arrangements are made, does that make life in the P rotocol environment even more difficult than you have already described, or does it remain equally difficult?

I think we were describing a no-deal or thin-deal case. The more one agrees with the European Union, whether in the form of a free trade agreement or in other mutual recognition agreements, the more checks between Northern Ireland and Great Britain one should be able to remove.

Can you be completely clear on this? Are you saying that the vast majority of the checks on Northern Ireland-GB trade could be eliminated by an FTA? If that is the case, why do people object to this P rotocol being described as a Northern Ireland-only backstop? Is that not what it is?

I would want to do a lot of research before putting a figure on the number of checks that can be removed. However, it is clearly correct to say that the number of checks can be reduced in this situation. It is unlikely that a free trade agreement will eliminate all checks; in fact, I cannot think of a thin free trade agreement in the style of the EU-Canada agreement that has removed all checks. It will not remove checks in their entirety, but some will be removed.
The P rotocol very much governs trade and implies the maximum level of checks which one could start to remove in other ways, such as through free trade or other agreements.

This gets into the area of how many pluses you add after Canada. This is about the level of regulatory alignment and whether the UK Government in their current position want that level of alignment with the EU as part of a free trade area or association agreement.

When you talk about the status of Northern Ireland, it exists now, under the P rotocol, in a position of deep alignment with the European single market. It is little removed from, say, the Norway model of how relations between the EU and a non-member state work in practice. In fact, in some ways, with the Court of Justice’s explicit involvement, it is almost a deeper form of alignment.

An FTA, as with the EU-Canada agreement, represents a very different form of alignment. It could take in a lot of regulatory areas, but when the UK Government talk about zero tariffs and zero quotas, that is in some ways quite an old-fashioned way to look at a trade agreement. Regulatory alignment is where a lot of those checks—
But does this not show the similarity between what has been agreed and the previous May deal, except that it is now restricted to Northern Ireland?

As I said in my opening comments, the very logic of Northern Ireland’s special constitutional condition was to militate towards some form of special arrangement for Northern Ireland. May tried to defy the logic of that unique circumstance, saying that we could apply this on a whole-UK level. The Johnson deal goes back to applying some form of Northern Ireland-specific arrangement. It is Northern Ireland-specific and it is one of deep alignment. It is very different from an association agreement, which would certainly apply in terms of trade between the EU and the rest of GB.
Dr de Mars, do you have anything to add here? It is a very important point.

The thing that I would stress about regulatory alignment, which I think is frequently misunderstood or missed, is that it is not enough just to have the same rules. We have the same rules now, obviously; we have not been able to change any rules since we ceased to be an EU member state. That is not good enough. It is about the overseeing architecture. It is the extent to which the EU has insight into what we are doing in practice that determines whether or not there is friction at the border. That is why the single market is so unique.

So, my answer on all these matters of regulatory divergence is that, if the EU starts to fear that the rules are changing and becoming more and more incompatible, friction at the border will increase. If the UK is adamant that there is no dynamic regulatory alignment on anything to do with the free movement of goods, I imagine that that implies that kind of divergence.

If we are not planning on diverging on, say, technical standards of manufacturing, I am not entirely sure why regulatory alignment, in that sense, would be problematic. It would be simplest, for the purposes of the border, if there were alignment with the single market on goods. Saying that we are diverging implies that, for now, the rules are broadly the same. Some risk-space checking might be appropriate but, as there is more divergence in different directions, all that will increase. The proposed free trade agreement will not address those increases in divergence unless there are commitments in it to some form of regulatory alignment.
Thank you very much. Before we come to our last question, I know Baroness Hamwee had a series of questions, but one or two of them have been answered in part.

Q16 I think that most of them have been answered, unless you can add anything on what is required to be put in place to make the P rotocol operative by the end of 2020. It strikes me that no one has mentioned technology. You are not technocrats or engineers, so you might feel that this is not for you, but is there scope for technological developments to minimise the requirements at the border?

As we ran towards the possibility of a no-deal exit, the Government formed the technical advisory group on alternative arrangements last summer. Essentially, all that has happened is that the border issue has moved. When 1 January 2021 comes, there will no longer be a land border on the island of Ireland; it will move to the Irish Sea. A lot of the work of that group should not go away, except we have stopped talking about it. I was looking for parliamentary Questions about it; I know it met through to September, but there have been no headlines or reports about its operation. As David mentioned earlier, things like trusted trader schemes or accreditation schemes were emphatically part of that group’s mandate. If we are looking to reduce friction at the sea border, that group needs to stay operative. The problem has not gone away, it has just moved.

Yes, there is scope for technology to play a role here. The problem with the discussion when we were talking about the Irish land border was that you still required a border, and border infrastructure. We are now saying that there will be border infrastructure on either side of the Irish Sea. Once you have that border infrastructure, it is possible to use technology to reduce levels of friction. I would be quite disappointed if the group that Colin referred to has been wound down. I was quite disappointed that the Alternative Arrangements Commission, set up to look at the Irish land border, then decided to stand down when the new P rotocol came in, almost as if it did not matter to the sea border. Actually, it should matter even more. I would very much like to see technology play a role, as it could in other UK ports of entry.
Trusted trader schemes and assurance schemes are all much easier to do in a sea border framework than they ever would have been with a land border framework.
Because you do not have 200 crossings.
But Micha e l Gove in hi s speech yesterday said that there would be an operational border. He said that it would take quite some time, maybe five years.
2025, I believe , is when he said the smartest border in the world would be ready.
If that applies at Calais/Dover, it applies equally at Cairnryan/Larne.
Q17 Article 4 of the P rotocol says that Northern Ireland is part of the UK’s customs territory and we can include it within the scope of any future FTA. What are the implications of that?

Yes, we are free to include it, but let us look both ways at this. Let us take an example of a country with which the EU does not have a trade agreement—say, the United States. Will the United States be happy to include produce from Northern Ireland going to the United States at reduced or eliminated rates of tariff when those products could have come from the EU without further checks? Well, we will see; the US could be quite sympathetic to Northern Ireland in that situation, but I would not take that as guaranteed. So, yes, we can include Northern Ireland, in the sense of Northern Ireland exports, but our trading partners might have different views.
That is complicated by the notion of equivalence in regulation as well. It is not just tariffs that matter.

It depends. I think that if the UK as a whole does not have equivalence with the US as a whole, it is not any more complex. The US will have its forms of checking produce anyway. I do not think that that is so complicated. If the means of reducing checks between the UK and the US have been introduced, some of those should be open to Northern Ireland exports as well. I am just flagging up that there may be some issues.

In terms of products coming into Northern Ireland and whether they are taking advantage of the new rules, the rules apply within the P rotocol. Again, a judgment will have to be made as to whether goods coming from elsewhere to Northern Ireland—not from Great Britain but from other countries—are at risk and will have to have the EU tariff paid before, if applicable, it is rebated. In that sense, you could argue that Northern Ireland will not get the full advantage, but it should still get some advantage from UK trade agreements.

In respect of EU trade agreements made with countries that the UK does not have agreements with, in theory Northern Ireland products that go into Ireland and are then exported to trade partners should qualify. However, that is a bit of a grey area. So I am sorry but it is not entirely clear.

The issue could be multiplied if you are a small or medium-sized enterprise. If you are a very big business, you will have the resources to try to understand these overlapping regulatory arrangements, but lots of businesses in Northern Ireland will not necessarily have that capacity.
Dr de Mars, do you have anything to add?

This is all theoretical. How it will work in practice we will just have to wait and see. As David indicated, as and when the UK concludes trade agreements with partners, especially ones that the EU does not have trade agreements with, this might become a very big problem or a very small problem.
We are deep into injury time but the ultimate supplementary will now come from Lord Kerr.

Q18 Can I cheat and ask two? First, what happens if all these unknowns are not known and settled with systems set up by the end of the year? We know that legally the UK Government are responsible for ensuring that they are all set up, but what happens practically on the ground if they are not?

Secondly, what happens four years out if the Northern Ireland Assembly refuses, democratically, to consent? The article seems to say that the joint committee will sort it out. What does that mean? If democratic consent is refused, this P rotocol arrangement will presumably fall, because we are a democracy—but what do you revert to? Do you revert to a frontier across the middle of Ireland? I do not know.

I will take the first supplementary. Apart from saying the word “confusion” in response to what happens if the arrangements are not in place, I would hope that the UK Government would unilaterally put in place what they thought was the best approximation of what had been agreed with the EU in order to eliminate the possibility of confusion. I would hope that they would say, “We didn’t agree. This is what we think it is. We’re going to just do that.” That would seem to be the pragmatic approach.

Some efforts towards implementation in that regard would at least stop it becoming a tit-for-tat situation, with the UK and the EU taking retaliatory measures against each other, which of course could never have happened when the UK was an EU member state. You cannot impose retaliatory measures against an EU member state.

On the second issue, if, four years out, the Northern Ireland Assembly takes that call, there is almost an unreality to the question in that the call is massive for the Northern Ireland economy. It is a one-stop question. There are no gradations of being in or out; you take this call and potentially everything changes as soon as that happens. It is a little like the retention of counterterrorism measures in UK law and the idea of an annual sunset clause. Yes, Parliament had a sunset clause and could at any point stop the UK having counterterrorism law throughout the conflict in Northern Ireland, but it never got close to using that power. There was almost a chimera of democratic accountability in the process.
Dr de Mars, I will give you the final word.

What will the J oint C ommittee do if Northern Ireland says that it no longer wants the P rotocol? Those are going to be the world’s most unpleasant discussions. I honestly do not know. This goes back to the pre-withdrawal agreement situation when we said that we needed an alternative to replace the backstop. We did not get very close to finding an alternative to the backstop when that was the goal. This is saying that we have something that resolves the border issue, but Northern Ireland does not want it any more, so now please find us something that avoids all borders for ever. I wish the politicians involved the best of luck, as I do not think that this is a legal matter per se.
Thank you very much indeed for a thoroughly absorbing hour and 40 minutes. We are very grateful to you for coming and for being so frank with us.

segs.tx: Select Committee on Economic Affairs
Corrected oral evidence: Building more homes —follow-up
Tuesday 4 February 2020
Watch the meeting : https://parliamentlive.tv/event/index/6cb687cc-cada-4e6b-8fe6-e99756ffb56a

Members present: Lord Forsyth of Drumlean (The Chair) ; Baroness Bowles of Berkhamsted; Lord Burns; Viscount Chandos; Lord Fox; Baroness Harding of Winscombe; Baroness Kingsmill; Lord Livingston of Parkhead; Lord Skidelsky; Lord Stern of Brentford; Lord Tugendhat .
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questi ons 1 - 9
Witnes se s

I : Liam Halligan, Economist, Author and Broadcaster; Dan Wilson Craw, Director, Generation Rent; Mr Warwick Lightfoot, Head of Economics, Policy Exchange; Professor Rebecca T unstall, Emerita of Housing Policy at the Centre for Housing Policy, University of York .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnes se s
Liam Halligan, Dan Wilson Craw, Warwick Lightfoot and Professor Rebecca Tunstall .

Q1 Mr Halligan, Mr Craw, Mr Lightfoot and Professor Tunstall, welcome to the Economic Affairs Committee. We are extremely grateful to you for coming today. We have two panels today. You are pr obably familiar with our previous report on housing. Perhaps I could begin by asking a general question. Do you think that the Government are on track to meet their target of building 300,000 new homes, and what might be done to ensure that those homes are of the best standard and quality? Having started to read your book, Mr Halligan, I know what you will say, so I would like to start with you.

The important thing for the Committee to grasp is that meeting a 300,000 target at a point in tim e in a particular year does not do anything to address the huge backlog of shortage that has built up basically since the end of the 1960s. Professor Paul Cheshire—I know that the Committee is familiar with his work—estimates that there is at least a 2 mil lion or possibly 3 million unit shortage in our housing stock. It is not just about meeting the target at a point in time; it is about achieving a sustained rate of housebuilding that reflects our natural demography and net immigration.

Secondly, the large-volume housebuilders know that politicians and journalists are increasingly interested in this subject. A lot of the uptick that we have seen in the last two or three years as this debate has hotted up—30,000 to 35,000 units of the late st annual increase—has been permitted development rights housing, which is the conversion of shops and particularly office blocks into housing. Sometimes these schemes can work well in relatively affluent downtown areas, but often they work very badly. I c an cite quite knowledgeable people who say that we are building the slums of tomorrow. That is particularly the case on the outskirts of London and in some of the traditional spillover towns in the south-east. Using permitted development rights to turn off ice buildings, which are often of low standard anyway, into housing is a one-off—you can only convert each office block once. Also, inexplicably in my view, the law says that if you convert office buildings, you can partition them so that you do not have t o meet the usual regulations on space or even on light and ventilation. This is a really big problem.

Therefore, I do not think that the Government are on course. As well as not relying on increases in housebuilding via permitted development rights—which not only do not include space and ventilation stipulations but also come with no related obligation on social housing, community infrastructure levy, S ection 106 or other aspects of community value that housebuilders are meant to meet—we have to look more fundamentally at the housebuilding industry. The top end, to quote this Committee’s report of July 2016, shows all the aspects of an oligopoly. The last time we had a proper OFT—as it then was—inquiry into the housebuilding industry was in the aftermath of Kate Barker’s excellent report in 2004-05. The report came out from the OFT in 2008 and was buried under the headlines on Lehman.

Regarding the extent to w hich the housebuilding industry became concentrated after that, the OFT said that it was okay for now but if it became more concentrated it would be a problem. However, it has become much, much, much more concentrated since then, with SME builders—particul arly the “S” builders—being pushed right out after the financial crisis. They are finding it very difficult to get hold of land.

That is why the housing market is broken. It is partly because of the way the market for land operates, as I outlined in my bo ok. I hope, Chairman, that you have got to that bit. If not, I can explain it. However, a big problem is that the big housebuilders practise contrived scarcity in particular localities. They go slow and r amp up prices as high as they can in the face of mas sive overextended demand. That, in my view, is the root cause of the now chronic affordability crisis in our housing industry.

I broadly agree with what Liam has just said. My first observation is that, although private housebuilding has increased quite substantially over recent years, affordable tenures have stayed fairly flat. We are still not building the homes that are needed for people on very low incomes who simply are not able to afford to pay market rents or prices.

Secondly, in t he past year or so, the number of new housebuilding starts has dipped. So, although the trajectory in recent years might suggest that the Government are on track, we might still see that splutter in the months and years ahead.

The key is to direct policy at building more affordable—by which I mean genuinely affordable—homes, where people on below-average incomes do not spend more than a third of their income on their rent. It is a situation that too many people are in. We have more than 1 million household s on council waiting lists, and that follows cuts to council waiting lists and eligibility. At the very worst end, we have 86,000 households in temporary accommodation. Those are the figures that we need to really focus on in ramping up the supply of new h omes.

I agree with the two previous witnesses that it is unlikely that the Government will achieve their target. But I think that we at the Policy Exchange would question whether the target is really worthwhile . The Government do not ha ve any targets for how many jobs there should be in the economy. There is a demand for housing—we have more people and more households, and incomes are rising—but over the last 50 years housing supply has not been able to keep pace with it. It is rather od d to set a national target for the number of housing units we will have.

We also think that you could achieve that national target but still have a lot of problems in the housing market because the housing is in the wrong place. You could have a lot of ho uses built where there is little demand for them. You need to expand the number of dwellings where people want to live, work and lead their lives. We are very clear that there is probably no form of public policy that can overcome the issue of positioning. Some people will want to live in a certain category of housing in a certain place. It will be very expensive and exclusive, and will set social limits on growth. There will be certain property markets like that but, overall, there are distortions in the U K property market which, in our judgment, come essentially from the planning system and a reluctance to enable people who own land to sell it to someone who wants to build on it.

This issue goes much broader than just housing. We have just published an im portant paper—at least, we think it is important—on planning. We argue very strongly that what is important is not just housing but the development of the economy and the development of public services. You need also to build a hospital, a school and a res idential care home. The last time I came to help your Committee, it was to talk about social care. Having been involved in building social care homes, I can assure you that the planning system is an obstacle. This is a very broad, structural problem in the UK economy.

I will finish by saying that, whereas 40 or 50 years ago you might have identified a series of structural issues that were plain and obvious to see, the one remaining cl e a r and obvious structural impediment that legislators and policymakers s itting in institutions like this might address would probably be the planning system. The OECD shows that we are unusual in relation to land use and planning, and also very unusual in being a very flexible economy ; one of the few remaining structural rigid ities is in the planning system.
Your report has been circulated to the Committee, and I am sure everyone has read it.

I am in the position of coming fourth, and I agree with most of the things that have been said. In some ways it is quite positive that you are finding consensus among us, but on the other hand , perhaps rather negative. I think we are saying a lot of the same things that you concluded yourselves in your report of 2016-17: we are not building enough home s, but to build enough homes is not sufficient , in any case , to deal with the housing problems.

We need houses of good quality that are affordable and sustainable, that can be maintained and that we would like to see in 100 years ’ time, unlike some of thes e converted office buildings that we are talking about. That is quite a big challenge, and in some ways the problem has got worse over those intervening years. Certainly, affordability has got worse and if you look at the most extreme end of the system, ho melessness has got much worse over the last 10 years.

We really are in a difficult position, and to some extent central government, researchers and so on , have gone around all the possible causes, all the possible solutions, but there are some we really do need to talk about more. We have talked about the planning system a lot and tried a lot of things with it , but really making a big effort on affordable housing and on homelessness are two things we could certainly do. We need to do something different, be cause what we are doing at the moment is not working.

I would like to put a big rider on everything we have all said , though, because to some extent Britain has never been as well housed, and we should not forget that. The quality of housing, the amount of housing, the space inside houses is better than it has ever been. We have addressed some of the really terrible housing problems that plagued us through the 20 th century, and that is literally embodied in all of us who have grown up healthier than the gen eration before partly because of that progress in housing. But, again, we do not need to stop now; we can continue making progress. Now we need housing that is sustainable and supports life in other ways, but we need to think quite dramatically. We can end homelessness, but we will not do so by following the kinds of policies we are following at the moment. It is going to be a bit more expensive and will take a little more effort.

Q2 First, we are revisiting this issue so that we can hold people’s feet to the fire to some extent, so bear that in mind. We are not just going over old ground ; we are doing this because it is a way of bringing the whole issue to the forefront. I s it simply a case of too few houses being built? Is that the real issue: we just need more to be built?

That is not the only issue. As Warwick said, you do not want to be building too many homes in the wrong places, where there is not the demand. We have been building more homes in Doncaster and B urnley than we have in Cambridge. It is not just about the number.
We did have a big policy of new towns at one point.

Yes, but we have not built new towns since the early 1970s—that was Milton Keynes —e ven though our pop ulation has increased enormously. For the purposes of conversation and making sure that there is not a complete consensus, I endorse what Professor Tunstall said but, on the other hand, we are building new-build homes now with the smallest living rooms sin ce the 1930s and our volume housebuilders are making margins of upwards of 30% on very old technology, which shows that there is no competition.

We have astonishing rises in the number of concealed households, particularly in urban Britain, which are not i ncluded in the estimates of the numbers of households that are coming onstream. The ONS recently changed its methodology for looking at the number of households, in a completely retrograde way, in my view, suggesting that if households are not formed, the demand for a house does not exist — that household does not exist. They do exist: they are living in someo ne else's loft. This is a problem.

It is partly about the number of homes, but also about homes being in the right place. New towns happened and were as sociated with the infrastructure—new schools and hospitals— precisely because most of the new towns were incorporated before the Land Compensation Act 1961 , which I think should be a major part of your investigations . It is at the centre of my book and was closely investigated by Clive Betts' s committee in the other place in 2018 and 20 19.

We do need to build more homes, I agree with Dan. When I wrote this book, I set out to write a love letter to home ownership, as a working-class person who grew up in a fi rst-generation owner - occupied home, knowing that the equivalent of Liam now would not be in an owner-occupied home. That is a big part of the problem. Yet , a lot of my book ended up being about homelessness and social housing, because, frankly, the more I looked into it, the more shocking the figures on homelessness and the lack of social housebuilding became. That is really where the human misery is: at the sharp end, notwithstanding Professor Tunstall's broader comments.
Home ownership might not be the answer, though.
I do not think it is either/or.
The council houses of yesteryear were—

With all respect, I think that is wrong. Home ownership is a way of giving people stability and security. It has been a tremendous engine of social mobility in Britain for most of the last century. We now have a rate of homeownership well below the EU aver age: there are only three EU countries below us. I personally think that it will be a national reversal in fortune when we go below half of households being owner-occupied. It became half in 1969, the year I was born, and on current trends we are heading f or 50%. We have gone from 73% to 61% in the last 10 years and are heading for 50% quite soon. I personally think that it would be a major misfortune if that happened.

It is about a lack of houses and a planning system that requires root - and - branch liberalisation of a most radical character . T h e planning system gives opportunities for the rent - seeking and oligopolistic behaviour th at Liam has drawn attention to so vividly in his book. This has not just happened in the housing market: do yo u remember the supermarkets in the groceries market? Do you remember how many i nquiries there were , when we were told there was no problem of monopoly in the supermarkets, it was all tickety-boo? Just do a trip to Aldi and realise that for many years , ther e was a monopoly being extracted there. We were very slow to get to grips with it and part of the story was the planning system limiting the number of shop spaces and so on.

When you have a defective framework of regulation, o bviously rent - seekers will tak e advantage of it. I can understand land banking and why, if you are running a housing business, you would have to behave in that way , with the constraints you are under, but it certainly gives you genuine opportunities to extract monopoly profits. I also think we should take advantage of the more energetic competition authorities we now have. We encountered their full personality in Lord Tyrie in the Corridor a little while ago. That is something we should be looking to as well .

I also think there are one or two very practical things—we were talking about them in the Corridor . I have an eye to the householder who buys a house and it has not been built very well. You would be surprised at how many new - build householders are dissatisfied with quite serious th ings that are wrong with their properties. I have no expertise in the practicalities of building, but when someone shows me a house where the ceiling and the wall have not met — an executive build o n a redeveloped estate , an old Ministry of Defence property in Plymouth — I can see that that is fundamentally wrong.

When you have an encounter with a plumber who says, “ I am going to have to do quite a lot of damage here, I am afraid" and he comes out and there is no damage and he says , "Actually, this was built in the 1960s, so we can get to the pipes quite easily. Mind you, if you go into a new house , they never build them with a view to maintenance" — it is those sorts of things we have to think about on behalf of the consumer.
So there is a need for better-quality housing, not simply more housing.
Yes, and a common-sense element.

May I go back to the very interesting point made by Professor Tunstall? You made a general point about the nation. Would you be able to differentiate between different regions of the country, or urban and rural areas? The point that you expressed is rarely heard, and I just want to get a feel for whether it can be applied generally to the nation or to regional, urban a nd rural areas and so forth.

The nation as a whole is better housed than in the past in terms of the space per person and the quality of homes. There are big differences between regions and between urban and rural areas. There is a greater concentration of housing problems in the big cities, although some housing quality problems—particularly to do with insulation and the cost of heating—are greater in rural areas, particularly where people have been using solid fuels and so on.

London is rather peculiar, because people pay the most for housing but have the smallest homes and share them the most, and lots of other housing problems are concentrated in London. I would never want to overlook the serious housing problems that we sti ll have and that are still causing people angst, illness and early death, but those are concentrated among small populations in certain areas—mainly the big cities.

Q3 There is a school of argument that supply is not the problem; it is just the financial markets, QE and other factors. Do the four of you think that that is convincing, or is it an exacerbation of a problem that is rooted in supply?

It depends on whether you are looking at house prices or rents. At Generation Re nt we are thinking about the well-being of renters. Our focus is on what rents cost and how we can bring them down. Over the past decade, rents have gone up by 19% nationally and house prices have gone up by 40%. Whereas you can think of rents as being pur ely to do with the supply of and demand for housing services, there is an extra layer of market behaviour going on with house prices. People see houses as an asset. The influence of low interest rates has driven house prices to rise much faster than rents. That is because a low interest rate means that you can effectively borrow more, and if you can borrow more, you can afford to pay a higher asking price for a house, and that fuels house price inflation. The other effect of a low interest rate is that ther e is really nowhere else to put your money to get a decent rate of return. That has fuelled the popularity of property as an asset, and it has brought more people into the market and fuelled house price rises.

If we are thinking about the well-being of re nters and others who need affordable homes, we need to think specifically about rents. There is a valid case to be made that it is not just about supply, but only in relation to house prices.
I should perhaps have declared my interest as the ch airman of a bank, as we are getting on to that subject.

There is a chapter in my book called “The No Shortage Myth”. This is a very convenient narrative for the big housebuilders and their in-house economists, who have made a very concerted effort to influence national newspaper columnists. I speak from personal experience. This is a story that a lot of people want to read. It says, “Oh, it’s fine. We don’t need to build more houses. We don’t need to sacrifice any of the green belt. It’s all down to QE”.

Part of the reason is QE. I cite a Bank of England report from early 2018 that was not particularly publicised. It says that about 25% of the rise in house prices since 2009 has been due to quantitative easing. However, there have been low in terest rates all around the world. There has been quantitative easing right across the European continent and America, but the rise in house prices in the UK is far, far sharper, and the affordability multiples in the UK are far, far more difficult.

Also, a lot of the no-shortage narrative—the narrative started after Labour asked a chief executive of a big housebuilder to carry out a review of the housing shortage, which was a bi t strange—relies on numbers relating to housing supply that include all the on e-off conversions that I have referred to. There is a difference between net additional dwellings and new homes added, and there is a different statistical series that the ministry puts out. Those net additional dwellings numbers in my view massively overs tate the real sustained increase in housebuilding, because a lot of them are one-off conversions of very low quality, as I said.

Also, to drive the no-shortage narrative, the housing demand numbers are artificially lowered by arguing that, if a household is not formed, that household does not exist. But it does; it exists within concealed households, of which there are now 1.2 million in London alone. That household exists in the fact that 32% of men between the ages of 20 and 30 now live in their childhoo d bedrooms. That figure is up from 20% just 10 years ago.

I believe that the no-shortage narrative is more than convenient; it is deeply disingenuous and self-serving on the part of the big housebuilders, who know that people like you and like us are now having a very serious look at this industry. I think that you should regard that narrative with extreme caution and scepticism.
Are you implying that people are trying to maintain house prices and that is what is driving it?

Yes, I am maintaining that it is a convenient narrative for a lot of politicians who do not want the grief of fixing the supply side of the housing market. They would rather come forward with ill-judged demand-side measures such as Help to Buy. That has been a big reason why there has been such a bonanza for the volume housebuilders at the top end, even though they are building very sub-standard homes in some cases. They get lots and lots of planning permissions—it is in their annual reports. There are now 1 mi llion outstanding planning permissions. The big housebuilders sit on them and that allows them to control housing supply in specific localities to keep the margins as high as possible and thus make more money building fewer homes.

Q4 Lord Livingston of Parkhe ad: I am deeply sympathetic to the point about the lack of supply. Of course, you can build housing. However, I want to ask a question of Mr Lightfoot and perhaps Professor Tunstall. I think that Mr Lightfoot referred it to initially.

I want to pick up on the point about family homes that are occupied by much older people who might well move into an assisted living-type of accommodation if it was available. Is there another part of this narrative, which is the availability of assisted or supported living f or older people and the freeing up of family homes?

That is slightly beside the point. What you need is wider housing stock and a wider range of choice for people. At the moment, there is barely an incentive for anyone to move out of a f our-bedroomed house into a two-bedroomed flat. When you go through all the transaction costs, you see your net saving and the permanent income that you will get out of what is left after moving and you ask yourself, “Why go to the trouble of doing it?” The next question is, “Do you want to live like a pig in a poke?” I have a lot of friends who are a bit older than me and all live in four-bedroomed, slightly unmanageable houses. They would all like to move to something a bit easier but the truth is that we do not want to live in a place where you cannot swing a cat and where space standards and so on are a problem. Sometimes it has been quite difficult for people getting planning permission from the planners to get permission to build bigger houses. You will find that there are a lot of constraints. There is the cost, which is the real key, but also sometimes the planners are not so accommodating when it comes to a roomier build.

This is a marginal issue. Going back to the Chair’s question, it is a complicat ed issue. You have limited supply and periodically you have monetary shocks. There was a monetary shock in the 1970s with the Barber boom, there was the Lawson boom and there were very loose monetary conditions before 2007. The Bank of England has often tu rned a Nelsonian eye to the impact of monetary policy on house prices. I think that the previous Governor, Eddie George, said that there was no connection.
I will come to house prices in my second question—we are going slightly off the page. Professor Tunstall, is this an issue that you see at all or should we, frankly, forget about it being a problem?

Yes, I think it is. I think that probably all four of us on the panel would agree that there is both a housing undersupply problem and a money excess supply problem. Both those factors are at play. The increase in house prices cannot be accounted for simply by the increase in popula tion. There is plenty of scope for policy in both those areas. The tendency has been to focus on just building more homes without thinking about who gets them and how much they will cost.

In my research, I have looked at how much space different groups of people have. Between 1981 and 2011, housing space inequality increased. If you were a dirigiste Government at the centre, you would say that this was inefficient or that you needed to reorganise our existing stock. Everyone has more per person but the gap has increased.

When you look into the processes to understand why that has happened, you find that it might be partly due to increasing income inequality, with a difference in people’s ability to access mortgages and finance and so on, but it is also par tly due to demographic issues, with an increasing number of people living on their own. It is also due to the housing supply, with a focus on larger homes, despite the changes that there have been since the 1990s and an effort to encourage developers to bu ild smaller homes.

We are getting a mismatch in the system between the kinds of households and homes that we have, and that ends up with people occupying more space than they need. They might want it and enjoy it but many older people, in particular, woul d like to downsize if that option was available, and that would allow more efficient use of the national stock.

Q5 I would like to explore with Mr Craw and Mr Halligan the issue of pricing. To what extent is this predominantly a L ondon and south-east issue? There is a different set of issues in other parts of the country. We are looking at this from a very London-centric perspective, where rents are particularly high compared with the rest of the country.

There ar e housing difficulties in all parts of the country. There are areas where the job market is not particularly good. It is particularly difficult for younger people to get a decent career and build up a pot of savings that they can buy a house with. That is taking place around the country. The percentage rise in the cost of the private rented sector has been fairly consistent. Even in the north-east, where house prices are particularly affordable, the cost of private renting has increased substantially. But w hereas in the rest of the country home ownership has fallen, the social housing population has fallen in the north-east and the private rented sector has moved in.

Beyond that, there are questions of quality. Are rented homes, in particular, being maintained well enough by landlords, and are people getting value for money in the homes they pay for? That is a bigger issue. It is an issue in London as well because land lords have power in the market and can essentially neglect their properties. However, there are different dynamics in different parts of the country.

The affordability crisis is most acute in London. The most basic metric, which is average house price to average earnings, was below four as recently as the late 1990s. Now, nationally the average is almost eight. In London, the average is 12—figure 2.6 in my book—but even in places like the south-west, the south-east and the West Midlands it i s above six. If you think that the usual multiple of earnings is three, if it is above six in the West Midlands, that means that two people earning full time, before you even think about childcare, cannot afford a house.

When I made my latest dispatches o n housing, it was about new-build homes, because I wanted to make sure that this was not just a south-east thing. The north-west, the north-east and the West Country are covered by chapter 7 in the book — “ New Build Nightmares”. We found that house prices were very, very high in all those areas, particularly for young couples trying to buy a house. These are often second and third-generation owner-occupying households. It is a source of great anguish for them and their parents that they cannot do what their parents did, even though their parents were semi-skilled or manual workers and they are graduates. As I said, we found that house prices were very, very high. The majority of the people we spoke to, even in the north-west and the north-east, relied to a d egree on the bank of mum and dad. That means that it is not progressive, because you might not have that option.

Also, because Help to Buy meant that they could buy only new-build homes if they could not afford more, the quality of the homes was very low, and not only in terms of not passing building regulations. We found that countless young couples were being thrust into homes that were unfinished by the volume housebuilders so that the sales could be reported for their quarterly earnings, so getting a s hare price bump that gave all the executives a nice Christmas.

If you think that it is just a London thing, have a look at “Beds in Sheds”—something else that was a complete diversion for me in getting my book written. I kept saying, “I’m going to finish it any day”, then I would discover something else. Beds in sheds is not just a London phenomenon. Brent Council was the first of many councils that now use heat-seeking drones over outbuildings in suburban homes to determine who is sleeping in sheds. There is a beds in sheds epidemic in Oxford, Salford, Liverpool and Bristol. This is not just about dodging council tax; it is about people living in squalor in damp outbuildings. It is happening in a big way in our country and none of it is in the national sta tistics or considered by my friends in the press who talk about there being no housing shortage.

Q6 Given the discussions on QE, I should declare my interest as well as the deputy chairman of the Court of the Bank of England, s o I will not talk about QE. I want to talk a bit more about supply. I am particularly interested in the panel’s views on where the land should come from to build more homes. If the consensus of the panel is that at least part of the problem is supply, it h as been suggested that more publicly owned land could be released for building.

To what extent do you think that it is in the gift of national government or local government to release publicly owned land? Or is the problem that these wicked and evil prope rty companies are land-banking all the land and we need to change the incentives so that they start building on land that they already own? Is it about opening up the green belt or is it about going upwards in our cities as opposed to outwards? Where do yo u think we would have the biggest impact on improving supply?
I have spoken a lot and, uncharacteristically, will stand back here.

There is a fundamental flaw in the planning system. Try farms. We need to make use of a l ot more farmland and should also examine the green belt. Of course , there are public sector organisations that own land that they would rather sit on and it is hard work making them disgorge it, particularly the Ministry of Defence. Some local authorities are slow off the mark as well.

When we talk about urban environments, I would just say that the burden of having additional houses should not just be in urban environments, where there is green space that becomes more densely used. I certainly think we sh ould consider going up in a nice way, not in tower block-land but nicely; higher but with greenery and parks around. You do not want local authorities to have the incentive to build on all the amenity that is within a city. That is very important, because those people who are already living in the cities, making their contribution to this, should not have their walks and parks taken away from them or compromised.
We have to think very hard about farmland. Do we really need to have so much farmland in Englan d and could we build on a lot more of it? And we need to think about the green belt as well.

With respect, it might be slightly the wrong question. It is a technical question about where we can lay our hands on land to build on to meet this year’s targets, but we should be thinking about which bits of land are the right ones to build homes on that are going to be right for the economy and for society , and will be good places to live in 100 years’ time. That could be all sorts of different kinds of land, but I do not think we will find some sort of treasure trove of land, certainly in public ownership at the moment, that is going to solve all our problems. Some of it is going to be in the wrong place; a lot of it is contaminated or quite remote, depending on what public sector use it had.
Is not the fundamental problem the price of land?
Yes.
What do you think we can do about that?
This goes back to some o f the points that Warwick has been making about how radical we want to be about private land ownership.
This is a very radical Committee. Try us.

It would be perfectly possible to nationalise land, if you are being ra dical, and to determine its use according to our concept of the public good or the economy’s good, rather than its owner’s good.
I think Warwick is having a bit of a coronary now.
How would you identify the right land for building, if your answer is to nationalise it?

How would you persuade the community, having identified that land, to accept it? Clearly, you could nationalise it and land these things, or you could find some way of coming to an agreement—identifying the land but also the process by which you are going to build on this agricultural land.

There are two thrusts of the work of my colleagues at Policy Exchange. One is the more liberal one of the planning system and land use. The other is recognising that we seem to have the worst of all worlds. We have control over land that means it is difficult to get new housing supply, but many communities are very dissatisfied with what stuff looks lik e when it gets built. Then there is the agenda of a more attractive environment that the late Sir Roger Scruton was involved in. My colleagues at Policy Exchange think that if you could enable communities to be consulted more effectively on the way things should look , in a manner that pleases them , rather than certain prominent architects, we might get more consent to some of the building.

The other thing would be changing the planning system and the scope for local communities and local councils to make de cisions on individual projects, which seems to me to be an opportunity for entrenched distemper. I was a member of a local authority for many years and I saw the extraordinary efforts that were made to have a row over the planning system. You are all famil iar with the arguments over Brexit, but I can assure you of the intensity of the arguments in local communities over the planning system.

The other factor is the ad hominem attack on anybody who wants to change anything or build anything. Whether it is changing a shop or replacing a bungalow with a very big garden which is hideous and half falling down with two very nice houses and two more manageable but nice gardens, the vitriol that gets driven into those people in their local communities is something to behold.
On the point about the cost of land, do you want to comment?

I will, if I may. There are one or two ha res running and I have one or two points to make that might be helpful to Baroness Harding, because this is a key political moment, I think. Yes, of course, building up is part of it, in an aesthetic way, as Warwick said. London has just 100 inhabitants pe r hectare. Madrid and Barcelona have well over 300. They are not unattractive places. Paris has more than 200. Again, it is not unattractive.

The first thing to say about land is that we have lots of it. Total residential buildings in England, including ga rdens—I only have the numbers for England— account for 1.3% of our land mass. There is an awful lot of space out there. The green belt, in contrast, is 13%, and it is not as if the green belt is being built on. The green belt is currently 168% bigger by acr eage than it was in 1979, because it keeps getting added to, a point that is not often made.

In terms of state land, the state owns about 6% of freehold land in the UK. Often, the Treasury does not want it to be sold because it wants the best possible pric e ; but when there is a shortage not of land but of land with planning permission to build on in the hands of people who are prepared to build— and all those qualifications—the price keeps going up, so it is very difficult for other departments to sell the l and. If the state released just one-twentieth of its land for development, according to my sums, there would be enough — at the current UK average density of 45 homes per hectare, which is low by international standards — to build well over 2 million homes. Th at would solve our housing crisis with one-twentieth of the state’s land, and we could build far more if the state-owned land was urban, which it often is, because you could build at a much higher density.

When it comes to the price of land and buying land , when you build a new-build home, the price on average of the land is 70% of the value of the home, which the household must service with an often bloated mortgage for the rest of their working life, in many cases, with mortgages going to 30 or 35 years n ow. In the 1950s, the land was 5% of the price of the home, even though we had already had planning permission through the Town and Country Planning Act.

The price of land is driven by speculation, because there is always an incentive to sit on land, so yo u have to do two things—and I speak as a free-market person, as many people around this table, many former teachers of mine and friends and colleagues, know me to be. First, you have to tax developers when they have planning permission on the land. Secondl y—
A return to a development land tax?

Yes, but it has to be a Conservative Government who do that, because we reversed it in 1961. Labour had three attempts at bringing back a development land tax and the market always felt that in the end, the Tories will reverse it. In fact, when the 1961 Act was reversed, the Housing Minister at the time, or just after, who tried to stop that reversal and go back to a situation where the state took some of the upside of the pl anning gain, was Keith Joseph. Milton Friedman supported him, in memos that I have found.

My proposal is not that we go back to the 1947-1961 regime, which was Attlee’s new Jerusalem, where the state took the whole of the upside when planning gain was pert aining. Of course, when you had big estates that were being hit by death duties and all the rest, it meant that they really did just sit on the land and you had to CPO them and have dogfights. If, as in many other countries, including Germany, the Netherla nds, a lot of the States, Australia, South Korea and Singapore, you actually split the gain in a meaningful, transparent way—which I would say would be 50 : 50, and the Chancellor agrees with me on the record in this book, by the way—then the speculation wil l come out of the land market. And crucially, to go back to your point, Lord Fox, the local authority will then have money earmarked for those schools, hospitals, doctors’ surgeries, children’s playgrounds, bypasses and new railway stations, to revolutioni se the local politics of planning.

People are vindictive, Warwick, as you know, because there is nothing in it for an existing resident in new build homes. It is more pressure on everything — it is noise; whereas if you had my mechanism of sharing the planni ng gain, you could get rid of S ection 106 and CIL, which is just a lawyers’ bonanza paid for by new homeowners and the state, and you would just have this very discrete, transparent sharing of the planning gain. Tony Pidgley of Berkeley Homes agrees with m e, as do lots of different people from across the spectrum. Local planning disputes would be far less divisive and vindictive, because a lot of the local population would want those new homes, because it would turn the place they live into more of a place. There would be more local infrastructure and better communications. Their house price could actually go up.

I am quite sceptical of all that, in the sense that I have seen plenty of arguments about the planning ga in being used for a loc al school. I can assure you that people do not always want a local school. The arguments you can have over a residential care home or a local school and its shape can be very intense. I do not buy this idea that there will be a game of happy families if yo u simply have a more effective way of capturing the ga in .

I query Mr Halligan’s comparisons. When you compare London with Barcelona and Paris, do you mean Greater London or Inner London? London is a very big place, if we take Greater London . I do not know whether the definition of Barcelona and Paris is the same.

The numbers I used—figure 2.12 in my book—are from the European Commission. I looked into them, because friends of mine reading drafts of the book asked exactly the s ame question as Lord Tugendhat. The definition that it used was inside the main périphérique road. That is inside the M25, so it includes a lot of suburbs and semi-rural areas. It is the same in Paris and Barcelona. London is not like Madrid, Paris and Bar celona, which have much higher densities. As I say, they have over 200 or 300 inhabitants per hectare respectively, but we have just 100. They have suburbs, too. So I think it is a reasonably fair comparison.

I am conscious of time, so we need t o move on to the next question, which Lord Stern will ask. I am a little confused about the idea of bringing in a tax. I cannot see how that will deal with the problem that such a large part of the cost of housing is in land. Indeed, you just argued that i t might actually result in house prices going up.
In relative terms.
Yes, but I do not really understand how this can help.

Chair, with respect, because it takes the speculative heat out of the market. You would hav e to combine it with CPOs in certain cases and with other measures, so that once developers have land, they have to use it within two years and finish the home, not just start it, which they do cynically. That brings more supply to the market.
Q7 The Chair: I can see how, as you say, you will have to pay a tax in five years’ time that might result in people offloading a whole load of land, which might reduce prices.

The question I wanted to ask you on house prices, which you more than hinted at in you r book, is this. If we were successful in reducing house prices and creating supply, what do you think the implications of that would be for financial markets and the wider economy? You suggest in your book that there is a kind of—you do not use this phras e—establishment conspiracy to not address this problem, because the fact that these high house prices are supported by a lot of debt makes it very difficult to solve the problem without creating a crisis.

There are two levels to that. First, it is just basic political analysis that politicians like high house prices and remortgaging—the feel-good factor—because it gives the economy a boost and home owners are generally more likely to vote. However, the political geometry is shifting. A lot of home-owning parents are very alarmed that their adult children cannot buy homes. We are destined for increasingly radical politics if we do not solve this problem.

However, you are right that there is a kind of deeper, less widely spoken and broken argument, which is that if you take real action to increase the supply of homes and house prices fall—given that I think around 70% of bank loans in this country are linked to property of some kind, often residential—there may be a concern that you are und ermining the solvency of the banking system.

I am not arguing to build half a million homes a year; we need to build more like 300,000 to 320,000. That needs to happen consistently or be the consistent average over time. What I am looking for is a normali sation of house prices. It does not need to be an absolute fall but a move back to a situation in which the average house price across the country is more like three or four times the average wage, rather than eight times, where it currently is.
An answer worthy of a Minister.

I want to come in on this point, and then I will ask about concentration. I have been teaching economics for 50 years; that is my job. If you look back over 40 or 50 years, during that period, inclu ding with the deregulation of the financial system, we have had more and more of savings and finance going into financing houses rather than investment. Adair Turner and many others have addressed this; Adair’s book, “Between Debt and the Devil”, focuses o n that story. We end up with the number you just described for how much of bank lending goes into the housing system. That is, in large measure, driving up the price of land rather than causing investment to take place. That is a problem that we have creat ed, not just in the UK—
I agree.

—but particularly here, over the last 40 or 50 years of deregulation in various shapes or forms. Would you not agree that that is something that we ought to address directly, for exam ple in restricting the fraction of the house price that a mortgage can be advanced on, and so on? Should we try to control how much of national savings and the national financial system is oriented into housing, thereby pushing up the price of land?

Liam H alligan: The economist in me completely agrees with you. It is weird being here having read all your textbooks over the years. However, the political analyst in me suggests that that is unlikely to happen. We are already seeing the return of large mortgage s. According to one headline, “The ‘monster’ mortgage is back”. Some providers are already lending at five and six times earnings. Some politicians will always reach for the easy solution of letting people borrow more.
Yes, but con trolling the fraction of the mortgage in relation to the house price is one way of dealing with this.
I would like to do that, but I cannot see it happening, I am afraid. I just do not think—
We are here to think of policies that work.
You are.
Policies in relation to the amount of lending going into driving up the price of land.

You need a suite of policies. Learned analysts and lawmakers such as all of you here need to keep the pressure on to stop people going for the easy route of more and more easy credit, getting up to lending at five and six times earnings and 110% mortgages, as was the norm before the financial crisis. We also need to ease the situation, not by stoking up the demand side with more Help to Buy, which could yet be in the pipeline—I hope not—but by easing the supply side and getting competition into it, so that we can build more homes and address the policy from all angles.
Lord Stern of Brentfo rd: You have to look at both the demand and supply side. It would be barmy to look just at one.
But you should not artificially boost the demand side in the face of relatively low supply, pushing young people into buying only new-build homes with disastrous consequences for quite a lot of them.
Understood.
Just before we leave this, do any other members of the panel want to come in?

You are absolutely right to think about this. The centra l banks will have to think more carefully and take some guidance from emerging market economies, not least the People’s Bank of China, on how you direct lending to small firms and try to divert it. I also think that, as part of our framework of monetary co ntrol, we need to think again about not just relying on interest rates to change price and demand but introducing an element of direct control i n the banking system to restrain a demand that we cannot deal with. Central bankers will have to get their hands dirty.
As will the Ministers of finance who instruct central banks.
Indeed.

If you wanted to do something with the financial system, you could look at discretionary investment in property—namely , the buy-to-let mortgage. You could restrict the availability of interest-only mortgages, so that you drive investment away from existing stock and into building new affordable housing, for example.

Q8 Yes. There is a whole range of policies there. Let me ask about concentration. My question is how it actually manifests itself in the market. Are the oligopolies so strong that these people are getting together in what we used to call smoke-filled rooms a nd stitching up markets? How does it actually work and what are the consequences?
The numbers are pretty incredible. I mentioned the 2008 OFT report. Volume builders, 2,000 plus, built 30% of homes in 2015, since when, anecdotal evidence wou ld suggest—
No, my question is about the manifestation of those concentration ratios and what actually happens.

Sure. In 2015 , volume builders went to 59%. I would not talk about conspiracies or smoke-filled rooms, but I do report testimony in my book from various local authorities which suggests that local builders are so powerful that, behind closed doors, they can negotiate away their S ection 106 obligations to provide affordable housing, to pr ovide local infrastructure and to make payments. Often, there are so few local housebuilders who can produce and can sink the capital in—
So it is power in relation to local authorities?

Yes: they are choosing not to impose the CIL, which, of course, is still discretionary. There is other evidence in my book that , of the headline rates of S ection 106 moneys and CIL moneys that are due, a very small proportion actually end s up being paid. Local authorities in the end f ace a choice—do you want us to build these houses in the next year or not? If they are not built, you will get into trouble with Whitehall.
How do you break up the monopolies or oligopolies? I understand that it is power in relatio n to the local authority, which is an important feature.

The first thing to do is to have an inquiry and get the numbers. It is very difficult now to get the numbers. I have tried very hard. Various industry bodies that used to provide them have suddenly stopped providing them.
What policies could you follow?

W e should actively help small businesses to get hold of land. Some of that state land I have talked about should be sold and earmarked specificall y for small and medium-sized firms. That would do something to bring about more competition and help get back to the situation we had before the financial crisis, when small and medium-sized builders were building the majority of our houses. That meant tha t they turned planning permissions around quickly, because of their cash flow and their employment intensity, and they built better homes because they rely on local reputation.
In other sectors you might require disposal of assets or prevent takeovers. I agree with encouraging SMEs, but that does not necessarily, by itself—
That is a possibility. I cannot get hold of concentration numbers beyond 2015, and I tried really hard. Until I see the numbers—
Lord Stern of Bre ntford: Suppose you could ; what policies would be available?

It may be that you would have to call for deconsolidation of what is now a very consolidated housebuilding sector in certain places. As I say, the picture is very opaque. The pictu re of who owns land in this country is extremely opaque, let alone who is building houses. It is very hard to get hold of these numbers.
Does any other member of the panel want to comment on this?

Very quickly, the difficultie s we hear about from smaller housebuilders are difficulties getting viable land, difficulties getting planning permissions and never getting Section 106 agreements. You have an oligopoly that has piggybacked on a defective framework of regulation and land use control, and that is the nub of what you have to get a purchase on if you are going to remedy this in a serious manner.
Lord Burns, I am conscious that we are running out of time.

Q9 Can we talk a bit about the rise of homelessness and how this fits into the story you have been telling, and the mechanisms? I am aware, having in the distant past tried to model the housing market in various forms, of the extraordinary endogeneity of it all. Ultimately, everything seems to affect everyt hing else and highlighting the root causes is quite tricky. What I would like to hear from each of you is to what extent this process we have been talking about has led to homelessness. To what extent has homelessness risen and what measures should the Gov ernment be looking at to deal with it?
I think this is your subject, Professor Tunstall.

You are absolutely right that everything is linked to everything in the housing world. It is a highly segmented market, but it is all one market in the end. If you focus on rough sleeping, it is quite a small problem in terms of numbers, although it is very significant for those people and for society as a whole. To that extent, it is much more specialised. Having stresses in t he housing system as a whole, around the affordability of home ownership and whatever, is linked indirectly to street homelessness. You can see that pattern if you look at the historical trends, but the immediate causes of street homelessness are a bit mor e specialised.

It does not help to have that context, but we know what causes street homelessness and we have done everything over the last 10 years to follow the recipe for creating a rise in it. It is about support from local authorities, funding for NGO s that work with homeless people, support for renters to pay their rent, housing benefit and universal credit and support for people who have specialised problems. We have done everything wrong, unfortunately, in all those areas, and the result is a very b ig rise in the last 10 years.

If you look at family homelessness, that is a much bigger problem in terms of numbers, and it is more directly linked to the stresses and strains going on elsewhere in the housing market: difficulties in affording home ownersh ip; difficulties in finding affordable private rented accommodation and staying in it. There again, unfortunately, we have done all the things that will make it worse, but we know that we have the recipe for reducing homelessness as well.

When it comes to reducing street homelessness, not only have more than 500 reports been written in Britain on how to do it ; we have successfully done it in the past. The Major Government had great success and reduced rough sleeping by half in three years. The Blair Governm ent had great success and reduced rough sleeping nationwide by two-thirds in four years. We can do it again; we just need to put a bit of money and effort in and reverse the policies that have put extra pressure on the system recently.
Then the re is the disguised homelessness, almost, that we have been hearing about, which is the sharing and the people who are still living with parents.

Yes: some colleagues of mine at Heriot-Watt University have developed a new concep t of homelessness that includes rough sleeping but also people sleeping in tents and cars, concealed households and people in inadequate temporary accommodation, and that number has also gone up greatly. They have done some modelling and quantified the lik ely impacts of various changes. They think you could reduce core homelessness by 22% in five years if all local authorities would provide prevention and support services to the same extent and quality as the best. You could also get large percentage change s if you rolled back some of the recent benefit changes, if you increased the provision of affordable housing, and so on.
What are the numbers of homeless in the UK on the expanded definition?

Shelter says there were 306,000 homeless people across the UK in 2018—that is rough sleeping and other forms of homelessness. That is up from 293,000 the year before and it is a tenfold increase since the early 1970s. Rough sleeping is separate, as Professor Tunstall says, and I too reco mmend the Heriot-Watt work, which is excellent. A lot of the reason why we have people falling into homelessness, be it bed - and - breakfast homes, temporary accommodation, families being split up—the sort of “Cathy Come Home” scenario—is that in many cases , we have stopped building social housing.

It fell under the Thatcher Government, but it was extremely low under Blair through Brown. Housing authorities are building about 25,000 homes a year. A lot of them are “affordable”, which means they cost 80% of mar ket rent, but 80% of market rent in Camden or central Manchester is not affordable. Many housing authorities build lots of social housing, which costs roughly 50% of market rent. It is not always 50%; there is a formula and an algorithm. Housing authoritie s are not building all that many social housing homes—council houses, if you like.

In the last couple of decades, we have shifted our focus in social housing from subsidising bricks to subsidising benefits. We are now spending some £25 billion on the housi ng benefit bill. Some of that goes to housing associations, but a lot goes to private landlords. Then, for understandable reasons, George Osborne capped the amount people can have in housing benefit, yet rents have continued to rise. A lot of people have f allen out of social housing because the state does not actually own the homes they are in. They are not secure. You are putting insecure and often vulnerable households, or plain low-wage households which want to do an honest job and in which both parents go to work, in a housing benefit situation, in which their housing benefit is one-third or a half of their rent and they just cannot make the rent.

We need urgently to reverse the ideological move to stop building council houses and put the borrowing and t he house on the state balance sheet, so that the state does not have to keep subsidising the mortgages of private landlord, buy-to-let empires and can actually build some physical, tangible homes. There will always be a need for one-fifth of the population to be housed in housing at submarket rent.
